title: Why cling
hookLine: people come together and part like travelers at an inn (Bodhicaryavatara 8)
tomorrow: what does everyone you'll ever meet want?

lines: AN INN ON A DARK ROAD.
cards: The arrivals gate at an airport. A grandmother has her arms around a grandson who's grown a head taller since she saw him last. A few steps away, a couple is saying a slow goodbye at security.
Same hall, same hour. People keep arriving and leaving, and nobody gets to keep anyone at the gate. Why hold on so tight, then?
Shantideva has a picture for this too. It isn't an airport. It's an inn on a dark road.

teach.b: Travelers meet at an inn at nightfall. They share a fire, a meal, maybe a story. Someone tells a joke and the whole room laughs.
In the morning, each goes their own way.

That, says Shantideva in the Bodhicaryavatara, is how beings come together in a life: each of us arrives alone, each leaves alone, and in between we lodge together for a while. So why cling? It sounds cold the first time.
It isn't asking you to love less. Watch the travelers again. A good inn is one where people are kind to each other, precisely because the night is short.
What he warns against is clutching: needing a friend to stay the same, to never take another road, to belong to you.
Clinging turns love into fear of losing it. The Buddhist word is upadana, grasping, and it's a closed fist.
Loving lightly is an open hand: warm, generous, and honest that morning will come. In the picture, nobody is wrong to leave at dawn. And nobody is wrong to have loved the evening.

how: Buddhist teaching on impermanence and non-clinging is often practiced through reflection on change and through loving-kindness meditation, which pairs warmth toward others with letting go of control.

o: a reason to keep people at a safe distance
a complaint about friends who move away
a question about holding too tightly to people

games.q: the inn on the road — tap the pairs.
p: a life, shared for a while

s: Shantideva says not to love people, since they'll leave
his picture is a kind evening at an inn; what he warns against is clutching.
in his image, people come together and part like travelers at an inn
each arrives alone, each leaves alone, and in between we lodge together.

games.q: your cousin leaves for a job overseas next week, and the family dinner is tonight. what does the inn picture suggest?
o: be fully there tonight: the stories, the jokes, a real goodbye.
skip it; goodbyes only make the leaving harder for everyone.
spend dinner convincing him to take a job closer to home.
games.why: the travelers don't stop the morning, and they don't waste the evening. love the dinner; let the road be his.

practice: Count three people who've shared your inn: someone in your life now, someone who has moved on, someone you met only once. For each, give one breath of thanks for the evening you had together.
Let your hands rest open on your lap while you count.

wordCard.voice: Why cling: Shantideva's question about people who meet and part like travelers at an inn. Love them; don't clutch.

carryVoice: Your line: travelers at an inn. A warm evening, an open hand. Chapter eight, underway.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 8.33-8.34 (born alone, die alone; like travelers taking lodging for a night)
